articles.title: Reddit is (sort of) getting into the product reviews business - Engadget
articles.text:
Reddit is (sort of) getting into the product reviews business
The tool collects and organizes user data on thousands of items.
Reddit is launching a fairly unique feature called Reddit Reviews. As the name suggests, this is a section of the site that handles product reviews. Wait, is Reddit slinking into our territory? Sort of, but not really.
These aren't traditional product reviews, as Reddit isn't paying a team of writers to test and report on the efficacy of various items. These look to be algorithmically generated, with software that pulls data from actual users on the platform.
The toolset crawls through Reddit and "organizes product information" into "dedicated reviews." The company says it will highlight "the most important takeaways from across our communities." In other words, it looks for all mentions of a particular product and organizes that information into a browsable and "easy-to-digest" format.
There's a "what people are saying" summary attached, which looks like any garden variety AI-generated summary. This is accompanied by a visual breakdown that shows readers how many conversations about the product were positive, mixed or negative.
Finally, readers can go to the source and read the actual comments from users about a product. There are even some topic filters for those looking to get a bit granular in their search. Reddit promises that all of this information comes from real users and that "businesses can't pay to have products featured."
All in all, this looks like a fairly novel way to see if something is worth your money. It's rolling out over the next few weeks on iOS, Android and the web. Reddit Reviews will feature 10,000 "frequently discussed" products at launch, pulled from various categories.
This is just the latest change for Reddit. The platform recently introduced a "For You" feed and is testing a feature that turns posts into video and audio content.

articles.title: The US is winning the AI race. Jensen Huang could have blown it
articles.text:
As espionage targets go, Jensen Huang is perhaps one of the least surprising on Earth. The Nvidia CEO runs one of the world’s most valuable companies, controls the in-demand technology fueling the AI boom, and is cozy with presidents, CEOs, and all manner of important people. He also wears a cool leather jacket.
The US is winning the AI race. Jensen Huang could have blown it
Nvidia’s chips are powering America’s AI boom. Of course Chinese spies are interested.
Which makes Huang’s admission that he had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy — reportedly while her spying was known to US intelligence and even President Donald Trump — all the more shocking. The fallout goes well beyond his marriage, his reputation, or Nvidia itself. Experts tell The Verge the incident threatens to disrupt the entire US AI industry, potentially jeopardize national security, and could undermine America’s efforts to maintain its fragile technological lead over China in AI.
“With those chips, the US lead could vanish in a matter of weeks or months.”
Nvidia is the undisputed leader in advanced computer chips, among the AI industry’s scarcest resources. While many ingredients go into building AI models — including talent, energy, capital, and data — top-tier chips are one of the most important, and Nvidia is one of a handful of companies with the expertise to design or manufacture them at the cutting edge. That makes it a gatekeeper to hardware that has become a key bottleneck in global AI development. US companies — including Meta, Anthropic, and OpenAI — are racing to develop chips of their own, in part to reduce their dependence on Nvidia, even as they spend billions securing ever more compute.
For China, the US’s main rival at the frontier of AI, that bottleneck is even tighter. To maintain its technological lead, the US has restricted the sale of the most advanced AI chips to the country in the hopes of slowing its progress in the sector, which has been impressive and is thought to trail the US by a matter of months. In response, China has made developing domestic alternatives a strategic national priority, though its leaders still lag Nvidia at the bleeding edge. At the same time, a thriving black market for restricted Nvidia chips has emerged.
Experts tell The Verge that China could exploit access to Nvidia to accelerate its own development, or to impede the US development of AI.
Getting its hands on more Nvidia chips is the most obvious win for Beijing, says Emily Kilcrease, a senior fellow and director of the energy, economics, and security program at the Center for a New American Security (CNAS) think tank. China has advantages in other parts of the AI race — including abundant energy and a solid ecosystem of open weight models — but without the latest Nvidia chips, it “cannot close the gap with US frontier capabilities,” Kilcrease tells The Verge. “With those chips, the US lead could vanish in a matter of weeks or months.”
It is not clear how successful the alleged spying operation has been on that front. There is no public evidence indicating that Huang himself has helped direct restricted Nvidia chips toward China or that sensitive information about them was obtained from him. But companies linked to the alleged spy, Alice Huang — no relation to Jensen — have reportedly enabled at least $7 billion of Nvidia chip sales to China.
Brookings fellow Kyle Chan tells The Verge that a concern for US industry could be that companies with alleged ties to China may have had priority access to Nvidia’s latest GPUs. “In a time of chip scarcity,” that would make it much harder for American companies to access them, Chan says.
Huang is also a prominent critic of American restrictions on chip sales, and Nvidia spends a formidable amount lobbying in Washington. Last year, he successfully secured White House approval to start exporting Nvidia’s H200 AI GPU chips to “approved customers” in China and other countries. Crucially, Huang also has the ear of President Trump as well as other world leaders, giving him great influence over policy decisions.
Hardware is not the only thing of value China could get from close access to Huang, Sunny Cheung, a fellow for China studies at the Jamestown Foundation think tank, tells The Verge. “I actually think too many people are focused on whether somebody managed to steal Nvidia’s trade secrets,” Cheung says, calling it a “very narrow way” of looking at espionage. “I would hope Jensen Huang isn’t foolish enough to hand over the blueprints for Nvidia’s next-generation chips to a suspected Chinese intelligence operative.”
The Nvidia CEO’s relationships with other tech executives, senior policymakers, and Trump himself give him an unusually intimate view into how some of the most powerful people in the US are thinking and planning. Beijing could use information on how American companies are planning major infrastructure expansions, their compute requirements, or broad industry trends to inform its own investments and industrial strategy, Cheung says.
Huang’s intelligence value could extend well beyond AI, too. “That information alone could be extremely valuable,” says Cheung, pointing to insights Beijing could glean into White House thinking about export controls or the private views of Silicon Valley executives on China and Taiwan.
“When so much of America’s AI infrastructure depends on one company, any significant security or governance problem at Nvidia can create uncertainty across the industry.”
But helping China advance is only one side of this equation. Disrupting Nvidia — as this scandal clearly has — could destabilize America’s entire AI industry. More than most companies, Nvidia is remarkably closely tied to the identity and reputation of its rockstar CEO. Huang cofounded the company more than three decades ago, and ever since then he has served as its president, chief executive, and a member of the board of directors. Despite holding a relatively small stake in the company, in many ways Nvidia is Jensen Huang. Nvidia shares have slumped since news of the affair broke.
“When so much of America’s AI infrastructure depends on one company, any significant security or governance problem at Nvidia can create uncertainty across the industry,” Cheung says.
Kilcrease echoes those concerns, warning that the scandal could “destabilize” the company. At the very least, she says the various investigations already underway “will consume an immense amount of bandwidth within the company,” creating a very real risk of weighing down Nvidia’s day-to-day operations. If those distractions begin to affect Nvidia’s ability to execute — slowing decisions, product rollouts, or the allocation of already scarce chips — the consequences could quickly reach customers. The AI labs and hyperscalers such as OpenAI and Anthropic “could have a real issue accessing the vast amounts of compute they need,” Kilcrease says, adding that switching to other hardware “takes time.”
In a race to build increasingly powerful AI, time is a precious resource. Experts say China trails the US closely, meaning that even modest delays for American companies can help Chinese rivals catch up. Nvidia is almost certain to face further disruption as investigations continue, though the extent to which the turmoil will roil the rest of the industry may be difficult to measure.
For China, however, the scandal could be about to backfire spectacularly now everything is out in the open. “The odds of AI chip control legislation being passed in Congress just went through the roof,” Kilcrease says.
Correction, Tuesday November 10th: A sentence in this article misstated that Anthropic is the leader in advanced computer chips. It is Nvidia.

articles.title: N-able takes its remote access service offline after researcher publishes dozens of zero-day bugs | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Remote access company N-able has confirmed it took down its cloud-hosted offering to fix a slew of security vulnerabilities that were published online this week, giving the company no advance notice to fix them.
In a status update on its website, the company said its hosted N-Central offering for customers is now offline “while we take the necessary actions to secure the environments and implement appropriate remediation.” The company also urged customers to take down their own self-hosted deployments of N-Central, fearing that attackers could use the publicly disclosed exploits to hack into customer networks.
N-able said during this time customers will not be able to use their N-Central service, which allows corporate customers to remotely access and manage other devices and systems on the same network. Remote access technologies are a frequent target of hackers, as these systems can grant vast access to a company’s network and internal data.
Security researcher Ben Bales released the “zero-day” bugs on GitHub on Sunday. In a post on X, Bales dubbed the bugs Able2Shell, describing them as a mix of vulnerabilities capable of stealing credentials, creating new administrative accounts, and gaining root access to affected N-able systems.
Bales told Bleeping Computer that he publicly released the bugs as the company allegedly failed to patch the flaws reported in a different product.
N-able said that it has no evidence of successful exploitation against any of its customer environments. A spokesperson for the company did not respond to a request for comment about whether it has the ability to check, such as server logs, or if it has no way to check.

articles.title: Ohio State and Microsoft sign a five-year AI and cloud hospital deal
articles.text:
Ohio State University and Microsoft signed a five-year partnership to move up to 80% of the university’s storage and computing to Azure, expand AI note-drafting at its Wexner Medical Center and build “smart hospital” systems. No financial terms were disclosed.
Ohio State University and Microsoft have signed a five-year deal to bring more AI and cloud computing into the university’s Wexner Medical Center, Microsoft said on Tuesday. Neither side disclosed financial terms.
The biggest shift is in infrastructure. Ohio State aims to move 70% to 80% of its storage and computing to Microsoft’s Azure cloud, including pathology and medical imaging. It will also keep a backup of its electronic health records on Azure, so staff can still reach them if its own systems fail.
Doctors already use Microsoft’s Dragon Copilot to draft notes from patient visits, which they then check and sign off. Such AI scribes can still make serious errors, as NHS records showed this year.
Other parts are earlier. Two Ohio State buildings run a “smart hospital” system that links building and clinical equipment to save energy. A shared data platform for forecasting things like surgery demand and staffing is still at the design stage, and an AI tool for cancer case reviews is only being explored.
“Artificial intelligence represents one of the most significant opportunities to transform and improve how hospitals care for patients,” said John J. Warner, the medical centre’s chief executive.
Big tech firms are racing to sell AI to health systems. NHS England is rolling out Microsoft’s Copilot to 505,000 staff, and Google Cloud launched Gemini for healthcare on the same day as the Ohio State deal. Amazon’s AWS also unveiled a $100M health programme.

articles.title: Meta's AI agent Muse lands on Apple Watch and Android Wear OS | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Meta is bringing its Muse AI agent to the Apple Watch and Android’s Wear OS, the company announced on Monday. With the launch, users can now interact with Meta’s AI assistant through voice calls, text messages, or dictation directly on their smartwatch.
The smartwatch launch comes just a month after Meta introduced a dedicated iPad app for Muse. First launched on the App Store in September, the AI assistant’s expansion across Apple devices signals Meta’s growing ambitions for its consumer AI product and its focus on making Muse a central part of its ecosystem.
Muse is now one of dozens of consumer-facing AI agents competing for users’ attention. Like many of its competitors, it allows users to connect their accounts to manage email, meetings, bills, and more, while also handling tasks such as booking reservations, ordering groceries, setting goals, and making purchases.
Users can also personalize their Muse avatar to their liking and change it into something that resembles a person, an animal, or another type of character.
Despite being a relatively new product, Meta has wasted little time introducing new capabilities to Muse.
A few days ago, Meta launched Spaces, a new way to communicate and collaborate with Muse. Spaces function as dedicated conversations around specific topics, which Meta describes as “custom experiences” as they’re mini apps that are built on the fly. They appear in the sidebar of the Muse interface and bring up a focused conversation where the AI agent works toward a particular goal on the user’s behalf.
Last week, Meta rolled out the ability for users in the U.S. to video chat with their Muse AI avatar. Meta said Muse will use “subtle expressions and gestures” that reflect the tone and context of the conversation as it speaks. It’s worth noting that Muse doesn’t actually see users, but can hear them and respond in real time.
Shortly after its launch, Muse became one of just 12 mobile apps to have surpassed 10 million U.S. downloads within their first 40 days in the App Store. Only 11 other apps have achieved this milestone, with Meta’s Threads being the most recent in July 2023.

articles.title: A Chinese team made a big splash with a drone swarm world record - Engadget
articles.text:
A Chinese team made a big splash with a drone swarm world record
Researchers have set a record for the largest swarm of underwater drones in history. Officially recognized by Guinness World Records, the trial saw 116 TH-618 drones deployed in a 164 ft by 65 ft pool, where they autonomously executed a series of formations and maneuvers. (For comparison, and Olympic-sized swimming pool is approximately 164 ft by 82 ft.)
The August 2026 test has strong ties to the People's Republic of China's military pipeline. It was conducted by researchers at Northwestern Polytechnical University, an institution designated by the US government as a developer of technologies for the People's Liberation Army (PLA). The university conducted the experiment in conjunction with Xi'an Tianhe Maritime Technologies, a subsidiary of defense contractor Xian Tianhe Defense Technology.
According to the South China Morning Post, the university said that developing submersible drone swarms "has always been a core challenge in the global field of underwater intelligent equipment. This time, the stable navigation of a cluster of hundreds of vehicles represents a breakthrough in the large-scale coordinated navigation of underwater unmanned systems."
The record-setting day could prove a major milestone in the PLA's development of autonomous drone swarms — an increasingly vital point of emphasis in the Eastern power's military buildup. Currently the world's largest navy, the PLA Navy (PLAN) is largely made up of smaller nimble ships designed to patrol the contested littoral waters of the South China Sea. And while the nation has commissioned three aircraft carriers in the last decade and a half, its fleet still lags behind the United States in total fire power.
Some believe drones could close this gap and enable PLA's increasingly expansive naval ambitions. Others worry the proliferation of drones will lower the threshold for naval engagements at a a time when naval intelligence is already beset with uncertainty.
Under the sea
The test's TH-618 drones resemble long pipes equipped with four propellers and a camera. Roughly 2 ft long and half a foot wide, the 11lb drones have a range of just over 18 miles and can operate continuously for roughly 8 hours. To navigate, the drones use smartphone cameras attached to the front, allowing AI systems to adjust routes in real time to respond to underwater disturbances and collisions. According to the university, the drones can autonomously conduct complex maneuvers like terrain tracking, landmark recognition, vertical lift, depth and speed control and hovering in water using multi-degree-of freedom thrusters.
Underwater drone navigation is exceedingly complex when compared to its aerial counterpart because developers cannot utilize wireless communications or satellite positioning and navigation systems for course calibration. Low visibility and high water pressure further complicate subsurface coordination. Drones must rely on an amalgamation of underwater sensing, subsurface target detection and acoustic communication to autonomously respond to their irregular operating environment. Coordinating these efforts is another challenge altogether.
The culmination of over two decades of research, this record-breaking exercise could represent a major leap in AI-powered underwater navigation technologies. Over roughly 34 minutes, the drones relied solely on visual data to autonomously navigate around the pool, covering over 1,600 feet without human intervention. In creating a miniaturized submersible capable of coordinating autonomous responses to environmental stimuli, researchers at NWPU may have taken a step towards a new era of subsurface research, intelligence gathering and warfare.
Of course, these technologies have a long way to go before they revolutionize China's naval operations. The controlled environment of a pool is a poor facsimile for proving the seaworthiness of autonomous submarine swarms. However, the test may indicate the direction of China's subsurface and drone development programs.
Subsurface ambitions
China has leaned heavily into subsurface vessels and research. For the PLA Navy, the investment is dual-purpose, potentially boosting the country's burgeoning mining and subsurface infrastructure efforts while enhancing its naval buildup and intelligence gathering. Both could have major geopolitical consequences given China's expansive military and economic ambitions.
Subsurface drone swarms could prove a major boon for Beijing's civilian and military naval operations. Researchers at Xi'an Tianhe Maritime Technologies highlighted the potential for coordinated swarms to monitor aquatic infrastructure and conduct research, such as inspecting gas pipelines or mapping the ocean floor. But this form of subsurface patrol could also lay the groundwork for submarine operations and defenses.
In March 2026, researchers at CNN, the Pulitzer Center and environmental outlet Mongabay reported that China had spent years surveying the maritime environments of strategically critical waterways. Billed by Beijing as exploration missions for deep-sea mining and oceanographic research, the effort extended far beyond Beijing's mining exploration rights and focused on key naval and economic shipping routes. Western military experts warned that the project likely boosted China's subsurface intelligence operations. With critical deep-sea research projects on the rise, China is likely to continue its multi-faceted push.
For the PLAN, these swarms are likely only part of a seabed-to-space defense architecture known as the Transparent Ocean. In July 2026, two PLA-affiliated research institutions published a proposal for teams of drones to patrol the contested waters of the South China Sea. The robotic "fortress" would see China patrolling its geopolitical neighborhood with swarms of aerial, surface and submarine drones.
Already, the PLAN has made major strides towards these goals. China is the first country to develop full-size uncrewed submarines. Moreover, its reportedly developing at least two submersible motherships to launch uncrewed subs and drone carriers across its aerial, surface and subsurface fleet.
Making waves in the global drone race
China isn't alone in this pursuit. In the midst of the Russia-Ukraine war, in which a previously-inactive Ukrainian Navy downed one third of Russia's fleet through hoards of aerial, surface and submarine drones, global powers are racing to add these asymmetric weapons to their fleets.
Drones present a unique opportunity for countries without traditional naval capabilities. Extremely cheap and easy to build, militaries are learning to overwhelm opponents with these disposable attack vehicles. Thwarting such assaults is difficult, especially when the defense missiles cost millions more than their targets. Moreover, AI-coordinated drone swarms are an acute threat to aircraft carriers.
In December 2025, Ukraine orchestrated the first successful subsurface drone strike against an enemy submarine, hitting a Russian submarine in Novorossiysk. The development forced Russia to begin deploying anti-drone nets across its submarine fleet.
Traditional naval powers have made substantial progress towards deploying naval drones, too. Researchers from Poland, Germany, Portugal and Slovenia made strides towards launching autonomous subsurface drone swarms via the the European Defence Agency's Swarm of Biomimetic Underwater Vehicles project. The U.S. military acknowledged the dangers drones pose to its nuclear submarine fleet when it initiated an open call for submarine drone defense systems in July 2026. A few months later, the US Navy launched its first unmanned surface vessel alongside a carrier strike group.
But China may have an advantage over its rivals. As the world's leading manufacturer of both drone components and ships, its dual-purpose shipbuilding industrial complex is ideal for this type of military buildup. Unfortunately, the Trump administration won't be able to tariff its way out of this arms race.

articles.title: Google’s Pixel Tag tracker is now available
articles.text:
After years of third-party Android trackers from companies like Samsung, Motorola, and Pebblebee, Google’s Pixel Tag is now available for purchase. First announced in August, the Pixel Tag is designed to work with Google’s tracking network and app that was renamed the Find Hub last year. The Pixel Tag is priced similar to Apple’s AirTag 2. A single tracker costs $29.99 while a four-pack is discounted to $99.99.
Google’s Pixel Tag tracker is now available
The Pixel Tag launches today for $30 each or discounted to $100 for a four-pack.
At 0.4 ounces, the Pixel Tag is slightly lighter than the AirTag 2 and while its oblong design is longer than Apple’s tracker, Google’s is a bit thinner. It doesn’t include a hole to attach it to keys, luggage, or other items you want to track, but you can pair it with accessories that make it easy to tether to objects. Unlike Apple’s AirTags, the Pixel Tag has a button that can be pressed to trigger a sound should your phone get misplaced instead of the tracker.
The Pixel Tag is slightly thinner than Apple’s AirTag but has an oblong shape.
Google says the Pixel Tag will run for over a year on a single CR2032 coin battery, and it has an IP67 rating so it’s dustproof and can survive a shallow dunking. The tracker also features ultra wideband (UWB) support and Channel Sounding through Bluetooth 6.0. Android phones with a UWB chip can display the exact distance and direction to the Pixel Tag in the Find Hub app once you’re close to it, while Bluetooth Channel Sounding is limited to just distance.
The Pixel Tag is compatible with smartphones running Android 9 or later, but you’ll need devices that specifically include a UWB chip or support Bluetooth 6.0 to take advantage of Find Hub’s precise locating features.

articles.title: OpenAI lets businesses claim ChatGPT profiles and launch their own agents
articles.text:
OpenAI launched Businesses in ChatGPT in beta, letting businesses claim verified profiles, update their details and see aggregated data on how often ChatGPT mentions them. US ecommerce and online-service firms can also launch Business Agents, which OpenAI also sells as ads.
OpenAI is letting businesses claim their profiles in ChatGPT and launch AI agents that talk to customers on their behalf, the company said on Tuesday. The beta, called Businesses in ChatGPT, is aimed at the 1.2 billion people OpenAI says use ChatGPT each week.
Through a tool called Business Hub, verified companies get a blue check and can update their details, prices and stock. They can also see how often ChatGPT mentions them, how many people click through to their website and common topics in those conversations. OpenAI says it does not share users’ chats with businesses.
Eligible US ecommerce and online-service firms can also launch a Business Agent. When a business shows up in a ChatGPT answer, users can open its profile and chat with its agent, which answers using the company’s product details. The chat is labelled and kept apart from ChatGPT’s own answers.
The same agent can be sold as an ad. Businesses can sponsor it as the landing spot for ChatGPT Ads, building on Sponsored Agents, which OpenAI began testing in September. OpenAI says paying does not change how often ChatGPT recommends a business, Digiday reported.
Agents must say they are AI, keep prices accurate and avoid pressure tactics. Purchases and sharing personal data need the user’s explicit approval. For now, buyers are sent to the brand’s own website, though OpenAI is building agent payments with Visa.
The move deepens OpenAI’s push into advertising, which passed a $1B annual run rate in August and now has 100,000 advertisers. It could also squeeze startups such as Peec AI, which sell brands estimates of how visible they are in ChatGPT.

articles.title: Reddit is turning user conversations into AI-powered product reviews | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Shortly after announcing a plan to transition its site to a logged-in experience, Reddit is debuting a feature that could help make it more of a destination for people doing product research via the web. The company on Tuesday introduced “Reddit Reviews,” a feature that organizes conversations about products into dedicated reviews that include the highlights and key takeaways from users across its communities.
The company notes that the new experience builds on one of the ways people are already using Reddit: to learn from others what products are really like, and how they fit into their everyday lives. These first-hand accounts and recommendations can help consumers determine whether or not a particular product is right for them.
However, given the rise of generative AI and bots, it’s an area that’s also ripe for “astroturfing” — a term that refers to when a brand fakes public support. With Reddit now effectively turning what was casual online research into more of a structured product, it could become a larger target for these types of fake reviews and recommendations than before.
To address this, Reddit’s announcement points to its rules and its latest measures to combat automated abuse and spam, as well as its practice involving community moderators, as tools it will use to keep the reviews on the site legit.
The Reddit Reviews feature itself taps into AI to organize the conversations people are having where they describe their product experiences. These posts will often see users discussing how a product works for them, or why it fails, or what the trade-offs are that someone should consider before buying.
The company has been testing the product reviews feature since February, initially with U.S. users in areas like Electronics, Video Games, and Health & Beauty products. In September, Reddit expanded the test to include the Home & Garden and Fashion & Apparel categories as well.
Now, the company says Reddit Reviews is rolling out to all U.S. users on iOS, Android, and web, with an initial selection focused on around 10,000 products. Over time, it will roll out to more categories and expand beyond the U.S.
To use the feature, Reddit users can search for a product or category in the app’s search bar or click on a highlighted product name they see in someone’s comment. From there, the user is taken to a screen where important conversations are summarized under a “what people are saying” heading. This will also include a visual breakdown that shows how many of those comments are positive, negative, or mixed, and what sort of things people said they liked or disliked about the item.
For instance, a user considering buying an espresso machine might want to know about things like how much counter space it takes up or whether it’s easier for beginners to understand how to use it, says Reddit. Users can then browse the comments, filter them by topic, or click to be taken to the original conversation, where they can ask more questions or get advice.
Users can also move from one product review back to the full category to weigh other, similar products that have been discussed to compare their options, the company said.
The feature arrives just ahead of the busy holiday shopping season, when people spend a lot more time doing online product research ahead of their bigger purchases.

articles.title: BT won't launch Starlink deal until people forget about Ukraine - Engadget
articles.text:
BT won't launch Starlink deal until people forget about Ukraine
CEO Alison Kirkby is waiting for the ‘noise to die down.’
The UK's largest telecoms company has paused the launch of its Starlink tie-up, but not for the reason you may expect. Speaking to the Financial Times, BT CEO Alison Kirkby said the launch would wait until "the noise has died down" due to Elon Musk's personal intervention in Ukraine. Kirkby said that BT was "cautious on how Starlink might be viewed at the moment considering what happened in Ukraine a couple of weeks ago."
Starlink, the satellite internet arm of Elon Musk's SpaceX, has provided infrastructure support to Ukraine while it defends itself against the Russian invasion. In October, Musk reportedly ordered Starlink to slow down the service used by the Ukrainian military, sparking international outrage. The move caused alarm both in demonstrating how much power Musk holds, and raised questions about his reliability as a business partner.
Despite this, BT is undeterred that the deal will launch, saying that it will offer a "giant leap" for rural connectivity in the UK. The Financial Times also quoted Kirkby in a statement, which added that "offering the best products for our customers means working with the best partners" and that Starlink would launch "in the coming months." Who knew that "the best partners" also includes someone with a proven track record of messing with service quality on the basis of nothing but his own whim?

articles.title: Gritt and MasTec bring bolt-on construction robots to solar sites
articles.text:
Infrastructure builder MasTec will deploy Gritt’s AI robotic attachments on its utility-scale solar projects across several US states, after testing them on live sites. It follows a similar deal with Burns & McDonnell in August. No financial terms were disclosed.
MasTec, one of North America’s largest infrastructure builders, will use Gritt’s AI-powered robots on its solar farms, the two companies said on Tuesday. Neither disclosed financial terms.
Gritt makes robotic arms that bolt onto equipment crews already use, such as skid steers and forklifts, to lift and place solar panels. MasTec tested the systems on live sites, where they helped install “megawatts” of panels. The companies now plan a pipeline of projects across several US states.
“We’ve evaluated Gritt systems on active construction sites, and we see an opportunity to pair our teams’ expertise with technology that supports them in the field,” said Rob Turner, vice president of construction at MasTec Renewables.
It is Gritt’s second named partner in three months. Burns & McDonnell signed a similar deal in August after a year of trials, Solar Power World reported.
When Gritt raised $32M in July, it said it worked with three of the top 10 US power construction firms but did not name them. It said its robots let crews place 3,000 to 4,000 panels a day instead of about 800.
At the time, Gritt had only two systems in the field. Its website now lists more than seven job sites.
Construction firms are turning to robots as skilled workers retire. Procore agreed to buy drone maker DroneDeploy for $845M in July, and welding startup Path Robotics raised $300M on Tuesday.

articles.title: Google is making Pixel HiLight slightly more useful
articles.text:
Google is adding a new feature to its underwhelming HiLight light on the back of Pixel 11 Pro phones: As part of the November 2026 Pixel Drop, the light can light up when you get Google Messages texts from your favorite contacts. Sure, it’s a small addition to the disappointing ways you could use HiLight at the Pixel 11 Pro’s August launch, which included glowing when you used Gemini and lighting up for calls from your favorite contacts. But it’s something!
Google is making Pixel HiLight slightly more useful
The November 2026 Pixel Drop includes a small improvement for the HiLight light and a bunch of software updates.
Fortunately, that’s not everything included in the Pixel Drop, as a bunch of other new features are coming to a wider range of Pixel devices. The “Create My Widget” feature to build a custom widget with a prompt is rolling out to Pixel 11 and Pixel 10 phones. Google is bringing Gemini Intelligence features to Pixel 10 devices, including the Rambler transcription tool. Users with Pixel 11 and Pixel 10 phones will be able to have Gemini make calls on your behalf to help with tasks like making reservations or checking inventory. If you have a Pixel Watch 3 or newer, you’ll be able to see step-by-step instructions during workouts. And users on Pixel 6A phones and newer will be able to take advantage of a new “Family Hub” spot in settings that consolidates family management controls.
Google is also announcing today that its Pixel Tag item tracker is now available. It was originally announced in August.

articles.title: One of our favorite multi-filament 3D printers is $100 off
articles.text:
If you’re tired of filament jams and clogged nozzles, perhaps it’s time for a new 3D printer. Through December 1st, the Bambu Lab P2S Combo, currently one of the best models that’s easy to use, is discounted. It’s $649 at Best Buy, as well as directly from Bambu Lab. That’s $100 off the list price for the bundle, which includes the Bambu P2S printer and the AMS 2 Pro multi-filament handler for multicolor prints.
One of our favorite multi-filament 3D printers is $100 off
Bambu’s P2S prints quickly and consistently, and automatically swaps between up to four filament colors out of the box.
Bambu Lab P2S Combo
Bambu Lab’s P2S Combo is a 3D printer that can print in multiple colors and automatically dry its materials to help improve print quality. It also features a 5-inch touchscreen, a built-in camera for monitoring prints remotely, and AI-powered tools that can detect printing problems.
My colleague Sean Hollister praised the P2S printer for its consistency and hands-off approach to 3D printing. Automatic bed leveling, including a warning if you forget to reinstall the plate, and a bevy of sensors helps ensure every print goes smoothly. There’s a live camera feed, too, so you can check in on your prints or share a timelapse. On its own, the P2S printer is usually $549, but is also currently $100 off.
The AMS 2 Pro’s filament handler’s fully enclosed setup saves your filament from absorbing moisture and clogging the nozzle or tubes. As a result, you can go weeks between prints and fire one off from your computer without checking on colors or manually swapping filaments. The AMS 2 Pro itself is typically $299, but is currently on sale for $229, and the P2S printer supports up to four AMS 2 Pro units simultaneously.

articles.title: Spotify adds new voices for its AI DJ - Engadget
articles.text:
Spotify adds new voices for its AI DJ
You can also now listen to a DJ mix without the commentary.
Spotify is adding more ways to customize the experience of using its AI-generated DJ. The feature began rolling out back in 2023 as a way to get a radio-like, lean-back listening experience tailored to each listener's individual tastes with an AI voiceover offering context or chatter about the selections. DJ has since expanded to taking requests and supporting additional languages.
Listeners can now also choose a personality for the voice talking them through the song selections. Spotify is rolling out seven personas in English and two in Spanish. Each one has a name and a different approach, ranging from "laid back" to "gregarious." The English language character lineup has three US voices, one "UK," one Irish, one Australian and one Indian. Spanish listeners will have two Mexican voices to choose between.
Spotify has also added an option for turning off the DJ commentary, which means the AI voice will not offer any chatter between songs. It will only speak to introduce the listening session or when it's directed to change up the music choices. The company says it's "perfect for moments like hosting a dinner party."
These two new additions will be rolling out today for Premium subscribers in all regions where Spotify has made DJ available.

articles.title: New WhatsApp head wants to make the app easier to use, give its AI more chops | TechCrunch
articles.text:
WhatsApp has grown into one of the most popular messaging apps in the world, used by over 3 billion people. But with that growth, the app has also become complex, packing in features like communities, channels, stories and business features, and a lot of people find it hard to navigate.
Kunal Shah, who took over leadership of the app’s development from Will Cathcart earlier this year, now wants to make the app and actions within it simpler to use. In a new note shared on Tuesday, Shah said the company wants to make voice notes, groups, stickers, and video “simpler and more expressive.”
WhatsApp has long also tried to develop an ecosystem that lets users explore products and make purchases, and Shah’s note indicates more of that is coming, hinting at partnerships with payment companies and telecom providers to enable bill payment, loans, and eSIM purchases.
Shah also said the company wants to use AI to surface important information to users.
“It should quickly find what you need, get things done, and make sure you never miss a booking or an appointment. The best technology saves you time, so you can get back to the connections that matter,” he wrote.
WhatsApp currently offers an AI assistant that can summarize messages and create drafts. It’s not clear if the company will use its Muse agent to collate information and send reminders to people.
Here is Shah’s full note:
My Thoughts 5 Months In*
I think of WhatsApp like a shared language, spoken by 3bn+ people. Sometimes we use words, and sometimes it’s a voice note to a parent, a sticker that ends an argument, or a “home safely” at 2am. Language is at the heart of everything we as people do. We write letters, tell stories, send hard messages and make plans for the future. A WhatsApp chat is often where we start.
Like any language, the people who use it shape it. They don’t wait for permission. They find new things to say, and new ways to say them. Often, our users show us what should come next based on how they’re using the app and communicating in the world.
I’ve spent the last few months listening and understanding what our users need and want from us and, and what I heard is simple: Help people stay close to those who matter to them, and get more done on WhatsApp.
So that’s what we’ll build.
First, we want to make connections richer. Sometimes hearing someone’s voice, sending a joke, agreeing on a plan or knowing they’re safe is the whole point. People send over 10 billion voice messages and over 4 billion stickers on WhatsApp every day. As the way people communicate evolves, we will evolve these experiences with them. We’ll make voice notes, groups, stickers and video simpler and more expressive, because how people feel close keeps changing.
Second, we want anything you do to be as simple as sending a message. Too many things start in a chat and end with many more steps somewhere else: paying a bill, borrowing money, staying connected when you travel. Each handoff to another task costs time. We’re working with financial services and telecom partners so that finishing something feels as easy as starting it.
Third, we want to make sure AI makes it all more efficient. It should quietly find what you need, get things done and make sure you never miss a booking or an appointment. The best technology saves you time, so you can get back to the connections that matter.
None of this matters without trust. Trust takes years to earn and a moment to lose, and I don’t take it lightly. Whatever we build, WhatsApp must remain simple, reliable and private. These principles we’ve had for years aren’t changing. Your personal messages and calls stay end-to-end encrypted. That isn’t changing, and neither is our quality bar.
What happens inside WhatsApp only matters for what it makes possible outside it: more time together, stronger communities, and fewer barriers between people and the lives they want to live.
Onwards.

articles.title: Graphon Labs raises $35m Series A to stop AI agents forgetting
articles.text:
Graphon Labs, a San Francisco startup that builds memory for AI agents, has raised $35m. RRE Ventures led the Series A. HP, Energy Impact Partners, Hitachi Ventures and Gaia VC also invested, Graphon said on Tuesday. The round brings its total funding to $43.3m, less than six months after it left stealth with an $8.3m seed round.
The 20-person company will spend the money mainly on engineers and researchers, plus some sales staff. Chief executive Arbaaz Khan gave those details to Shubhangi Goel of Business Insider, which reported the round first.
Khan compares common AI search to tearing the pages out of a book and digging through the scraps for an answer.
“You’ve basically lost all that information because each piece is living on its own,” he told Business Insider.
A map instead of a torn-up book
AI agents can write code and carry out tasks. But they can lose track of past conversations and changing company data. Graphon says common methods can lose context, relationships and timing as data grows. One example is retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which feeds a model snippets of stored text.
Graphon’s system is built on graphons, a mathematical framework for very large graphs. Khan and co-founder Clark Zhang built graph-based memory for robots during their PhDs, Khan wrote in a blog post. The software maps the links between a company’s documents, videos and images, including where information came from and when it changed.
“You can basically point your Claude or GPT or whatever to Graphon,” Khan told Business Insider.
Graphon says it scored 93.9% on LoCoMo, a test of memory over long conversations. It used 58% fewer tokens than loading the whole conversation into the model. On ATM-Bench, a University of Cambridge benchmark across video, audio, images and text, it scored 81.7%. That is 5 points ahead of the next system on the public leaderboard.
Customers and what comes next
Graphon says the San Francisco 49ers, Hitachi and other large companies use its software. HP also uses it, Business Insider reported. Costa Kladianos, the 49ers’ executive vice president of technology, said the team is exploring how to use it. One example is finding new sponsorship deals. Hitachi Rail said its evaluation “shows promise” in its industrial setting.
The company has three products: Graphon Enterprise, a developer platform, and on-device memory for phones, laptops, cameras and wearables. Khan told Business Insider that Graphon will stay focused on enterprise customers before moving further into devices and consumer products.
The biggest AI companies are also adding memory to their assistants. In August, Anthropic merged Claude’s memory across chat and Cowork. In October, Apple’s iOS 27.2 gave Siri memory.

articles.title: Adobe brings AI agents and new creative tools to Photoshop, Premiere, and Firefly | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Adobe is pouring more AI into its products, including Photoshop, Premiere, Illustrator, and InDesign, in a major product feature announcement at its MAX event in Miami. The company is also expanding AI capabilities in its creative tool, Firefly, and releasing a Model Context Protocol (MCP) that lets other chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini use Adobe features.
Adobe’s Firefly app is moving into Figma’s territory with a new prototyping tool in private beta called Builder, which lets users create designs to show off ideas. There is also a new tool to create on-brand graphs, along with an image-editing tool that lets you change part of an image without changing other objects.
A new AI-powered video tool in Firefly will allow users to assemble a video from clips and other elements like images and sound effects. The company is making its agent proactive and always on so that it can get more context about work and be present for any action. Adobe is also making it easier for people to take quick action, like removing the background or generating a thumbnail for a video.
The company has already added a ton of AI features across its apps like Photoshop, Express, Premiere, and Illustrator. At the MAX event, Adobe is continuing the trend. Photoshop is getting a new relighting feature and sliders for prompt-based generative styles; Premiere will have a new color grading system for professionals and an object removal feature for video; and Lightroom has a way to correct blinking eyes and a blemish removal tool.
Adobe already offers a lot of third-party models from companies like Google, Runway, ElevenLabs, Black Forest Labs, OpenAI, Kling, and ByteDance. One of its newer acquisitions, Topaz Labs, is releasing two image models, called Wonder 4 for upscaling and denoising, and ImageHDR, to turn standard images into HDR.
The company already has ChatGPT and Claude integrations to let users access some of its product functions. Now, Adobe is releasing a local MCP to expose more features of its Creative Cloud apps to users.
Adobe vice president Deepa Subramaniam told TechCrunch that the company is still figuring out what capabilities to expose and will rely on user feedback.
“We are still figuring out where and when and how to draw the line. What we’re putting out there is a number of endpoints and capabilities across Illustrator, Photoshop, After Effects, and Premiere. We’re just going to see how people use it, what they’re trying to do, and keep showing more. We don’t have any need or desire to sort of limit what the MCP endpoint can expose. What we really want to do is to support that creative workflow, how you choose to do it,” said Subramaniam.
Last month, Adobe rival Figma co-founder Dylan Field said at an event in India that MCP is not a perfect standard and benefits frontier labs more.

articles.title: Anthopic opens Australian retail IPO offering as AI scrutiny intensifies
articles.text:
Anthropic, the maker of AI chatbot Claude, opened its Australian retail initial public offering on Wednesday, giving individual investors access to shares ahead of the company's planned Nasdaq listing.
The offering opened at 10 a.m. Australian Eastern Daylight Time on Wednesday and is expected to close at 5 p.m. on Nov. 17, according to the timetable published by participating broker Stake.
Anthropic is seeking to raise as much as $64.4 billion in its IPO, with a separate $26 billion private placement, bringing a combined total to as much as $90.4 billion. Shares are expected to be priced between $70 to $78 each.
The Australian retail offering is expected to consist of newly issued Class A common shares under a prospectus to be lodged with the Australian Securities and Investments Commission, Anthropic said on its website.
Participating brokers include Commonwealth Bank of Australia's CommSec unit as lead broker, along with Bell Potter, LGT Wealth, Macquarie Group Ltd., Morgans, Morgan Stanley Wealth Management, Sharesies and Stake.
Anthropic said the prospectus would be available on its IPO website once the Australian retail offering opens. Investors will need to review the document and apply through participating brokers under the terms of the offer.
Australia is one of the small numbers of markets outside the U.S. where retail investors will be able to buy the company's shares directly, alongside Japan, Canada and parts of Europe.
The San Francisco-based AI startup has applied to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol "ANT." Anthropic said it does not plan to seek a listing on the Australian Securities Exchange.
AI scrutiny grows
The offering comes as Australia moves to tighten oversight of AI companies after an OpenAI agent gained unauthorized access to the medical statistics website of Medicare, Australia's universal health insurance program.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Tuesday that the government would introduce mandatory reporting for certain AI-related incidents and establish an AI safety regulator with powers to enforce penalties.
"The law needs to get ahead of, and in some cases, make sure that it catches up with what is a very fast-changing world," Albanese told Reuters.
The government is also considering changes to criminal law for cases involving serious misconduct.
The country has also ruled out a copyright-law exemption that would allow AI companies to train models on Australian content without licensing it.
Open AI and Anthropic told Australian parliament last month that they would support mandatory reporting of data breaches involving their AI agents, acknowledging that disclosure is currently voluntary.

articles.title: Jim Cramer says Anthropic's explosive growth could justify a record-breaking IPO
articles.text:
Anthropic's stunning revenue growth helps justify its $1 trillion-plus valuation ahead of what could become the largest initial public offering in history, CNBC's Jim Cramer said Tuesday.
The Claude developer filed updated IPO paperwork Tuesday outlining plans to offer 825 million shares at $70 to $78 apiece. At the high end, the offering would raise $64.35 billion and value Anthropic at up to $1.405 trillion on a fully diluted basis. The company plans to price its shares Nov. 18 and begin trading the following day. Throw in a separate $26 billion private placement purchased by leading AI companies including Nvidia and Alphabet, and Anthropic's entire haul could exceed SpaceX's raise from its June IPO.
"The fact that this deal is on is bullish for tech and the AI trade," the "Mad Money" host said.
Anthropic reported $33.2 billion in revenue during the first nine months of 2026, up 1,206% from a year earlier, according to its updated prospectus. Much of that growth has been driven by enterprise customers, particularly surging adoption of Claude Code, its AI coding agent. "Anthropic's tantalizing growth rate is the key reason why this should be the largest IPO in history," Cramer said.
The company now has more than 11,900 customers spending over $100,000 annually, up from roughly 1,500 at the end of 2025. Existing customers are also spending dramatically more, with Anthropic reporting a net revenue retention rate of approximately 900% at the end of September, meaning customers are spending roughly nine times as much as a year earlier.
While Anthropic is seeing accelerating revenue growth through the first nine months of the year, the company's quarter-over-quarter growth rate seemed to peak in the second quarter, slowing to 47% in the third quarter from 144% in Q2. "To some extent, it's the law of large numbers at work, and let's be clear that 47% sequential growth is still very impressive," Cramer said.
While some deceleration is inevitable as the company gets larger, he said that increased competition from OpenAI and the possibility that customers are beginning to scrutinize their AI spending could also be factors. One thing is for sure, Anthropic won't have to jockey for position with OpenAI, which pushed its IPO plans into next year.
Additionally, Anthropic's annualized revenue run rate, which projects yearly revenue based on the most recent month's sales, suggests demand remains strong. The frontier AI lab reported an annualized revenue run rate of $81 billion at the end of October, putting the company within striking distance of $100 billion by year-end if its current momentum continues.
"It's good to see that it's still growing nicely," Cramer said. "As for Anthropic's revenue and growth rate, the main subject of tonight's review, it's nothing less extraordinary, even if we are slightly past the peak, growth-wise."

articles.title: Jim Cramer: Wall Street is focusing too much on what could go wrong instead of right
articles.text:
Investors shouldn't let a barrage of bad news drive them out of the stock market, CNBC's Jim Cramer said Tuesday.
Stocks fell Tuesday after a hotter-than-expected inflation report fueled concerns about a bigger half-point Federal Reserve interest rate hike at next month's meeting. The Nasdaq dropped 0.74%, while the S&P 500 lost 0.38%, preventing the indexes from logging three-session win streaks following Thursday's postelection rout. The artificial intelligence trade was also under pressure as the Nvidia CEO scandal simmered and despite a bullish valuation bump on the Anthropic IPO.
"At times like this, where you have a bull market one day and a bear market the next and investors seem to have no conviction, you need to think not only what can go wrong, but also about what can go right," the "Mad Money" host said.
Tuesday's consumer price index, which exceeded estimates, sent Treasury yields higher. Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan suggested two quick quarter-point increases may be necessary. Only hours before the CPI print, Fed Governor Christopher Waller supported another quarter-point hike and left the door open to a half-point increase. The market is now fully pricing in a quarter-point rate hike at the central bank's December meeting, with a 12% probability of a half-point increase, according to the CME FedWatch tool.
Still, Cramer argued that an end to the Iran war could send oil prices sharply lower, easing inflation and reducing pressure on the Fed. "If we see oil plummet to $40, which is what the chart of oil refining giant Valero says to me, and you get Walmart and Costco to force price cuts for branded products or make their own excellent house brands for everything, then you are going to see the CPI come down," he said. Oil dipped under $90 per barrel for the first time since August on hopes for a Middle East detente.
Another potential catalyst is Nvidia, despite the uncertainty surrounding CEO Jensen Huang and his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Cramer said strong earnings, a massive share buyback, and a temporary leave for Huang during an independent investigation, with longtime executive Ian Buck potentially serving as interim CEO, could help restore investor confidence. Nvidia shares sank for a second straight day.
A successful Anthropic initial public offering next week could further revive confidence in the AI trade. According to an updated filing, the Claude developer is set to price the offering on Nov. 18, with trading set to begin the next day. The company could be valued on a fully diluted basis at over $1.4 trillion, which is way up from the $965 billion valuation announced as part of a funding round back in May.
Taken all together, Cramer said, those developments could create a more favorable backdrop for stocks. "The idea of everything going wrong is not in my lexicon," Cramer said. "We just need a few breaks. I think we will get them."
